blocks.text: >> On a Sunday morning in January 1987 India came to an absolute stop. Buses stopped on the roadside, markets were empty. People gathered around TVs. Many decorated with fresh flowers. Most had never read Valmiki Ramayana's 24,000 verses in Sanskrit, but they knew the story of Rama. How did a story written in a language most people couldn't read reach almost every corner of India? And here's something even more surprising. The people who ran

Doordarshan weren't sure the Ramayana belonged on national television. Long before printing presses, scholars wrote every verse of Ramayana onto dried palm leaves. Making one copy took months of labor. So very few people owned the copies of Ramayana. These manuscripts were mostly found in temples, royal libraries, and with wandering sanyasis. But if most people couldn't read the epic, how did they know the story? Because the Ramayana was also meant to be heard. According to tradition, Valmiki himself taught the poem to Rama's twin sons, Lava and Kusha. The

two boys traveled around singing the story, eventually reaching Rama's court. They became associated with the Kusha Lava, traveling bards who carried Ramayana from place to place. The tradition of singing and reciting Ramayana continued through generations. During Navaham, people gathered at night to listen to the story. King Bhoja even composed Champu Ramayana in a simple Sanskrit style called Draksha Paka. As the time passed, regional languages and dialects evolved across India. While Sanskrit remained the classical language of the epic and a common language of

communication across Indian subcontinent, ordinary people spoke and understood their own regional languages. So how did Ramayana reach to people who didn't speak Sanskrit? Local kings began supporting poets who retold the epic in language that ordinary people could understand. They also saw Ramayana as a way to instill moral values among their subjects. And soon different regions began developing their own versions of Ramayana. In Karnataka, the poet Nagachandra, also known as Abhinava Pampa, wrote an early Kannada Jain version of the Ramayana. In Tamil Nadu,

Kamban composed Tamil Ramayana. In Bengal, Krittibas Ojha retold the story in Bengali. And in Odisha, Balarama Dasa gave Ramayana its own Odia telling. By the 16th century, during the height of Mughal rule, traditional Hindu institutions were facing growing pressure. It was during this period that Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, a language spoken in northern plains of India.  His work gave people a way to experience the Ramayana in their own language. He used rhythmic chaupais and dohas that

people could easily remember and sing. Traveling kathavachakas carried these verses to temple steps, village squares, explaining the story in words that ordinary people could understand. Thousands of kings ruled different parts of India. Some kingdoms grew into vast empires. Their borders changed, and their rulers came and went, but something connected these regions. The sacred geography of the Ramayana. Let me explain. People traveled across the regions to visit places connected to Rama's journey. And these weren't isolated temples or local shrines.

Together, they formed a network of pilgrimage sites stretching across India. In the north, pilgrims visited Ayodhya and river where Rama crossed the Ganga. They walked through the forest where Rama spent parts of his exile. Near Nashik, people visited the place where Rama, Sita, and Lakshmana made their forest home. But the journey didn't end in north or central India. Down in Karnataka, people visited the boulder-filled terrain and caves of Kishkindha, the kingdom of Vanaras. In Telangana, devotees traveled to worship Rama at Bhadrachalam. And at Rameshwaram, people worshiped at a place

where Rama is believed to establish a Shivlingam. Before setting out towards Lanka, just off the coast lies Ramasetu, the bridge that Rama's army is said to have built across the sea to reach Lanka. People traveled across these regions, visiting the sacred sites and carrying stories back to their own communities. By connecting Ramayana to their own hills, caves, rivers, and coastlines, people across India made their places part of sacred pilgrimage tradition. But the Ramayana's influence didn't stop at pilgrimage. In Chhattisgarh, members of

the Ramnami community tattooed the name of Rama across their bodies as an expression of faith. The influence of Ramayana also shaped how people understood the leadership. Rama became the ideal king and the idea of just and righteous rule came to be known as Ramrajya. People greeted each other with Ram Ram and when someone spoke of moral boundary that must never be crossed, they called it Lakshman Rekha. But this tradition so deeply rooted in India's everyday life would face a very different challenge under British rule. Traveling musicians, mendicants, and storytellers who took epic from village

to village were increasingly viewed with suspicion by British. Some communities were even classified under criminal tribes. The pressure extended to education. Before British, indigenous village schools taught children Ramayana and other Itihasas. But the British began replacing them with English medium schools run by Christian missionaries. Even the temple administration was taken over by the British. The story however found an audience through cinema. In 1917, Dadasaheb Phalke made a silent film called Lanka Dahan.

People took off their shoes outside traveling cinema tents, threw coins at the screen and dropped to their knees in prayer. But ever since independence, an English educated left-leaning intellectual elite in New Delhi treated India's sacred heritage with deep  suspicion. To them, ancient Hindu epics were backward, embarrassing, and superstitious. They went on to occupy influential positions in India's universities, publishing houses, and cultural institutions. By the 1980s, a new medium offered another opportunity to bring Ramayana into people's homes. Television. A filmmaker named Ramanand

Sagar wanted to make a series based on the epic. But getting on to Doordarshan, India's national broadcaster was far from straightforward. Officials were hesitant. They were worried that broadcasting a Hindu epic in prime time could be seen as a remark on secularism. But SS Gill was on Sagar's side. He was the top civil servant at Information and Broadcasting Ministry and he had approached Sagar the series in September 1985. Gill later said that Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi asked him whether Hindu epic would cause a backlash. Gill

disagreed. To him the Ramayana was not about one religion. It was a story that belonged to every Indian. The deadlock broke and approval was finally granted. On January 25th, 1987 at 9:30 on a Sunday morning the first episode of Ramanand Sagar's Ramayana was broadcasted on Doordarshan. [bell] What followed was extraordinary. Streets emptied, families garlanded their television sets and folded their hands before Arun Govil who played Rama. The series became a national phenomenon.

Every Sunday morning millions of people stopped what they were doing just to watch Ramayana. At its peak it was estimated 80 million people tuned in. The story had traveled through manuscripts, village squares  and cinema screens had entered the homes of entire nation. The Ramayana has always moved into newest medium of its time. Nearly 40 years after Sagar's Ramayana, Namit Malhotra's Ramayana has brought the epic to the big screen. But the critics calling this a politicized version of the Ramayana. The film turns Ravana into misunderstood gentleman. It

recast Devas as the oppressors and the Rakshasas as the oppressed. It changed the moral conflict at the heart of the epic. No one expects every filmmaker to reproduce Valmiki's Ramayana word to word. Creative freedom is part of the tradition. Countless poets brought their own interpretation to the epic. They added their own creativity, their own literary styles and their own perspective. But they never abandoned the moral heart of the story. That reading of Ravana does not come from Kamban or Tulsidas. It comes from left-leaning retelling of the epic. When

cinematic adoption does that it raises a bigger question. Have we changed the way the story is told or have we changed what the story is trying to say? The Ramayana survived because every generation found a way to tell it while preserving its central moral conflict. Today cinema has that responsibility because how we tell Ramayana now will shape what the next generation understands about it.
